live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37): a long-running espionage group focused on Korea, per vendors
next.in_short: NICKEL FOXCROFT, also tracked as APT37 and ScarCruft, is described by several vendors as a North Korean espionage group. It mainly targets South Korea, using shortcut-file lures, cloud-based control channels and Android spyware.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this group as NICKEL FOXCROFT. Other names include APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces and RICOCHET CHOLLIMA.
CrowdStrike describes RICOCHET CHOLLIMA as a North Korea (DPRK)-nexus targeted intrusion adversary. It says the actor has run espionage operations since at least 2016.
Lookout describes ScarCruft as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group active since 2012. ESET calls it a suspected North Korean espionage group operating since at least 2012.

The line between this group and the Konni and Kimsuky clusters is disputed. Genians says some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group, while the MSMT report as cited by Genians assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct.
CrowdStrike says observed operations have almost exclusively targeted South Korea. It assesses the focus to be government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists.
AhnLab's ASEC says the group targets individuals such as human rights activists, reporters and North Korean defectors. It says the aim appears to be data theft.
Genians reported a March 2025 spear phishing campaign against activists focused on North Korea. The lures imitated a South Korean national security think tank.
ESET reported a game-platform compromise aimed at the Yanbian region of China. It infers the main targets are ethnic Koreans there, most likely refugees or defectors.
360 Advanced Threat Research Institute says a RokRat campaign targeted government personnel and corporations in South Korea and Asia.

Zscaler says the group has used Windows shortcut (LNK) files as an entry point for years. 360 and ASEC describe phishing lures where an LNK file starts PowerShell and loads the RokRat backdoor in memory.
One analysis says RokRat uses pCloud, Yandex and Dropbox as command-and-control channels. It can run commands, collect files and capture screenshots.
ASEC reported an attack on an old Hangul word processor flaw, CVE-2017-8291. The payload was hidden in a JPEG image and installed a backdoor named M2RAT, which logs keystrokes and takes screenshots.

Lookout attributes the KoSpy Android spyware to ScarCruft (APT37) with medium confidence. It notes that North Korean groups share infrastructure and techniques, which makes attribution harder. The apps posed as utility tools.

Zscaler described a campaign called Ruby Jumper, published in February 2026. It spreads through removable media to reach air-gapped networks and uses Zoho WorkDrive for command and control. Zscaler says that, to its knowledge, this is the first time APT37 has abused Zoho WorkDrive.
ESET says ScarCruft trojanized Windows and Android parts of a video game platform and delivered the BirdCall backdoor. It says the attack was probably under way since late 2024.
Genians named the March 2025 spear phishing campaign Operation ToyBox Story. Malicious LNK files in ZIP archives delivered RoKRAT, and Genians says its investigation is ongoing.

Zscaler ThreatLabz, in a report published in September 2025, described APT37 infection chains using a shortcut or help-file lure. They dropped the Rustonotto and Chinotto backdoors, followed by the FadeStealer data-theft tool.
Treat unexpected shortcut files inside ZIP attachments with suspicion, even when the lure looks relevant to your work.
Control removable media on sensitive networks, and monitor for PowerShell activity and unusual use of cloud storage services.
